source.title: Predictable Scaling Laws of Optimal Hyperparameters for LLM Continued Pre-training
source.authors: Yongwei Zhou; Jun-Cheng Diao; Jun-Lin Shang; Pei-Wen Li; Rong-Xiang Weng

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper’s main sections, references, and appendices; no truncation or garbling affecting the reported findings is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a loss-compute scaling law attributed to Kaplan et al. as an input to its continued-pretraining hyperparameter-prediction framework. Its own scaling results concern optimal learning rate and batch size, not the claim’s loss laws or parameter/token compute-optimal split.
record.gate_note: The paper reports regressions of compute against optimal learning rate and batch size, and validation-loss trajectories under selected hyperparameters. These are related findings but do not measure the loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute power laws, small-run loss extrapolation, parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, or downstream predictability named by the versions. The downstream benchmark scores and grid-search cost comparisons evaluate the proposed framework, not those claim versions. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper adopts a Kaplan-style loss-compute law L(C)=L0+αC^-γ as a tool to compute equivalent pre-training compute and predict optimal learning rate and batch size for continued pre-training. It reports no fit quality, exponents or extrapolation check for that loss law. Its own scaling results concern optimal hyperparameters versus compute, a related but different construct. Downstream scores evaluate its hyperparameter predictions, not scale-performance predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors add that 'equivalent pre-training compute', derived by inverting a loss-compute law, lets them predict LR and batch size zero-shot for 8B/3B checkpoints. They report a 70–92% cut in search cost with comparable or better benchmark scores.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a continued-pretraining framework for predicting learning rate and batch size from proxy-model mappings and an equivalent-compute estimate; it does not reproduce the original loss-scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimal-hyperparameter regression slopes differ between Dense and MoE architectures. The paper also reports different outcomes across learning-rate and batch-size settings, but does not provide a sensitivity analysis of the claim’s loss-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In continued-pretraining proxy runs, optimal learning rate falls and optimal batch size rises with compute. The slopes differ between Dense and MoE models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal LR and batch size scale predictably with compute in continued pre-training, with architecture-dependent coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batch and smaller LR reach lower terminal validation loss despite slower early progress.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal batch size grows, and the optimal LR shrinks, as training approaches convergence.

record.problems: The proxy scaling analysis uses only 100M and 500M activated-parameter models. The provided text does not give the numerical loss-compute fit parameters referenced in Appendix C, and Table 7 omits the R² values it says are summarized. Figure 4 results are qualitative and do not state the model identity or numeric losses. The authors also acknowledge that validation beyond Dense-8B and MoE-3B, and calibration for highly specialized domains, remains to be investigated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 downstream benchmark ablations and Table 4 search-cost comparisons were not extracted as rows because they evaluate the proposed hyperparameter framework rather than the loss-scaling or parameter/token allocation versions of the claim. Cited results in Related Work were also excluded.

untested.parts: The loss-compute power law is assumed and fitted, but no fit quality, exponent values or range are reported.
The loss law is used to back out Cpre for 8B/3B checkpoints. Whether it predicts large-run loss is not checked.
Continued pre-training is a different regime, but the paper reports no test that loss follows a power law there.
Downstream scores compare hyperparameter settings only.
The limitations section speculates that γ and L0 may differ by domain, but this is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The loss-law parameters (L0, α, γ) are never reported, even though Appendix C is said to contain them. The benchmark score differences between configurations are small (e.g. 51.3 vs 51.1) and have no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test held-out loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Does not test whether loss laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Studies optimal learning rate and batch size, not the compute-optimal parameter and token counts or their growth with compute.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count for their effect on loss.
Studies continued pre-training on text, but does not test whether the claimed loss power law transfers across modalities or the listed training regimes.
Reports downstream benchmark evaluations for hyperparameter configurations, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

Reports architecture-specific scaling of optimal learning rate and batch size in continued pre-training, but does not test setup or fitting dependence of the claimed loss exponents or parameter/token compute-optimal split.
